description: We are a team of passionate students with a shared interest in physics, astronomy, and computer science. We are motivated by curiosity and a desire to innovate. We enjoy combining scientific exploration with technology to develop creative solutions to real-world challenges.
summary:
Problem: A successful Moon landing depends on more than reaching the surface. A lander needs sunlight to generate electricity and a clear view of Earth to communicate. Both conditions change with location, surrounding terrain and landing date.
Solution: LunLux is an interactive website that lets users explore these conditions across ten lunar landing sites, including historic missions and possible future landing locations. Using NASA position data and elevation maps, it works out when the Sun and Earth are visible above each site's real skyline. A nearby ridge can block either one, so two similar-looking locations can have very different outcomes. At one candidate site, moving the landing point about one kilometre more than doubled the time Earth stays in view.
Users can compare landing dates, see how a delay affects a mission, and explore the results at two levels: a visual experience a young learner can follow, and a detailed analytical view for researchers and mission planners.
LunLux turns complex lunar data into information people can understand, test and use for planning and education.
details:
Detailed project description

What does LunLux do?

LunLux brings lunar sunlight, Earth visibility, terrain and mission timing together in four interactive sections:

  • Tour: introduces the solar system and explains what each body does, or does not do, to a lander on the Moon.
  • Explore: shows ten lunar sites on a 3D Moon, with terrain-aware sunlight and Earth-visibility results, an interactive horizon view and mission estimates.
  • Compare: evaluates sites and landing dates side by side, so users can compare conditions, adjust priorities and see the consequences of a schedule change.
  • Learn / Report: a visual explanation of lunar conditions in Educator mode, or detailed calculations, charts, sources and downloadable data in Researcher mode.

One switch changes the whole site between Educator and Researcher reading levels without changing the underlying data.

How does it work?

LunLux uses hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory Horizons system, covering 2026 through 2029.

For each of the ten locations, we built a complete 360-degree terrain skyline from elevation measurements made by the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

The system compares the position of the Sun and Earth against this local skyline to decide whether each is visible, blocked or close to the horizon. This matters most near the lunar south pole, where sunlight arrives at very low angles and small differences in terrain change the answer.

From these hourly results, LunLux works out the share of a stay spent in sunlight, the longest period without sunlight, the share of time Earth is visible, and the longest gap without a view of Earth. In Researcher mode the stay can be 1, 3, 7 or 14 days.

We also developed an adjustable six-factor score combining sunlight, Earth visibility, interruption lengths, clearance above the skyline and tolerance to landing-date delays. This score is our own comparison tool, not an official NASA rating.

How did we verify our results?

We built twelve automated check scripts that test the critical parts of the system, including the position data, terrain horizons, visibility calculations, mission metrics and what the screens display.

We also queried NASA JPL Horizons by hand and compared seven site-and-time results against our data. All seven agreed within 0.0004 degrees.

We compared our eclipse calculations with NASA's published lunar eclipse predictions for 2026 through 2029. Our data finds nine of NASA's ten eclipses directly; the tenth is a faint grazing eclipse that our model misses by under 1%, because it does not include Earth's atmosphere.

The model also reproduced real terrain effects that we never programmed in, including the valley walls around Apollo 17's landing site.

These tests helped us tell genuine physical effects apart from errors in data processing or display.

Limitations

LunLux is a planning and education tool, not a complete mission-safety assessment.

Sunlight does not guarantee electrical power, and a view of Earth does not guarantee a working radio link. Our power calculator gives estimates from stated assumptions, not a full spacecraft engineering model.

Each site is one geographical point, so nearby terrain variations are not fully explored. The project does not model lunar temperatures, dust, landing hazards, hardware failures or detailed communication link budgets. Custom coordinates are not yet supported.

Results are based on hourly data and the resolution of the available elevation maps. The 3D Moon is a visual; terrain blocking is calculated and shown separately in the horizon view.

What's next?

Future development could let users choose any lunar coordinates, evaluate many positions within a landing region, use higher-resolution terrain, and estimate power generation and communication performance more realistically.

We also hope to add thermal conditions, surface hazards and spacecraft-specific requirements, to make LunLux a more complete lunar mission-planning environment.

Tools and technologies

LunLux was built with TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js, Vite and Node.js data-processing scripts. The slides use Reveal.js. The site is deployed on Vercel, with source code and version history on GitHub.

Scientific inputs include NASA JPL Horizons, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation maps, NASA planetary reference data, NASA eclipse predictions and published lunar landing information.

Use of AI

We used AI assistants extensively throughout the development of LunLux, under our direction and review.

AI coding assistants wrote the code: the scientific data processing, the calculations, the terrain-horizon method, the analysis panels, the automated check scripts, the website's interface, the 3D Moon and the slide deck. They also wrote most of the on-screen text, including the child-level wording and the tour captions, which we reviewed.

We also used AI chat assistants for project planning, reviewing approaches, drafting instructions for the coding assistants and checking their work. Some suggestions were adopted; others were changed or rejected after discussion.

The tools were Claude Code and Claude (Anthropic) and ChatGPT and Codex (OpenAI).

The project's direction and final decisions were ours. Together we chose the scientific approach, selected the ten locations, defined the comparison criteria, chose the LunLux name and visual identity, set up the two reading levels, and made 37 recorded project decisions.

We checked results by hand against NASA's own system, tested the website, reviewed AI-generated work, and decided when each milestone was acceptable.

Our aim was not to have AI generate a website, but to use AI-assisted development while keeping responsibility for the science, the verification and the design.

The LunLux logo and wordmark were not AI-generated. An AI assistant cleaned up the image file and cropped the browser icon from it. We did not use an AI image, video or audio generator anywhere in the project. The diagrams are drawn from our data by AI-written code, which is acknowledged in the repository README.
